content.title: About
content.content: Duck sauce (5051) is a sweet‑sour condiment made from soy sauce, vinegar, sugar and aromatic spices. It is commonly used in Asian cuisine, especially with duck, fried dishes and sushi rolls. The sauce has a thick consistency, dark amber color, and a distinctive aroma with hints of ginger and garlic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “Duck sauce” comes from its traditional use with duck meat in Chinese restaurants.
Fruit extracts such as pineapple or apple are often added, giving a subtle fruity sweetness.
In Japan a similar condiment is called “tenkasu sauce,” though the spice blend differs.
Gluten‑free versions replace soy sauce with tamari.
The sauce is believed to balance the richness of fatty dishes by adding a bright, tangy note.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Soy and spices provide antioxidant compounds that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Vinegar and ginger stimulate gastric juice production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sauces, Duck sauce is low in fat, making it suitable for lighter diets.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: The sauce contains soy sauce, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar makes the sauce caloric; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Soy sauce is high in sodium; those with hypertension should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Duck sauce is served as a dip for duck, fried chicken, sushi rolls, and vegetable appetizers. It can be mixed into marinades, salad dressings, or used as a glaze during roasting.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a tightly sealed bottle in the refrigerator after opening. At room temperature it can last up to 3 months, but once opened it is best used within 1‑2 months. Discard if the smell or color changes.
